prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Knowledge is Power. That is what the billboard says and I agree. I am an adult, therefore I understand the threat of passengers. The threat to Our Children, who don't understand the threat of these bird-like, twitchy people. They pose two kinds of threat. To begin with, there is the one we all know about, the preda­tory threat, the hawk-like passengers that prey on children as they sit in front of their computers or televisions. The terrorist threat. That threat is easy to handle. You shoot it. You contain it. You confiscate. You stitch. You bleed from various orifices and sockets, but you survive, you rebuild house and rinse the child. The more serious threat is the diseases passengers carry with them. Internal terrorism. Children love those diseases. It makes them babble like possessed. Their make-up looks like oil in the moonlight. Such children cannot be cleaned off. Kill them. Or turn them into entertainment. Art.

outputs.L1:
“Knowledge is Power.” That is what the billboard says, and I agree. I am an adult; therefore, I understand the threat posed by passengers—the threat to Our Children, who do not understand the danger presented by these bird-like, twitchy people.

They pose two kinds of threat. First, there is the one we all know: the predatory threat—the hawk-like passengers who prey on children as they sit before their computers or televisions. The terrorist threat. That threat is easy to manage. You shoot it. You contain it. You confiscate. You stitch. You bleed from various orifices and sockets, but you survive. You rebuild the house and rinse the child.

The more serious threat lies in the diseases passengers carry with them: internal terrorism. Children love those diseases. They make them babble as though possessed. Their makeup resembles oil in the moonlight. Such children cannot be cleaned. Kill them—or turn them into entertainment. Art.
outputs.L2:
The billboard proclaims that knowledge brings power, and I share that belief. As an adult, I recognize the danger passengers represent—especially to Our Children, who cannot comprehend the menace posed by these nervous, birdlike figures.

Passengers present two distinct dangers. The first is familiar: predators resembling hawks, hunting children while they sit before televisions or computers. This is the terrorist danger, and it is relatively straightforward to address. Fire upon it. Restrain it. Seize it. Sew up the wounds. Blood may pour from different openings and sockets, yet survival is possible; afterward, the house can be reconstructed and the child washed clean.

Far worse are the illnesses passengers bring—the terrorism that operates from within. Children are drawn to these diseases. Infection makes them chatter as though possessed, while their cosmetics gleam like oil beneath moonlight. Once children reach that state, they cannot be scrubbed clean. They must either be killed or transformed into a spectacle—into art.
outputs.L3:
The narrator endorses the slogan “Knowledge is Power,” suggesting that informed adults recognize the danger posed by the beings known as “passengers.” These passengers are depicted as bird-like predators that target children through computers and televisions, turning familiar forms of technology and media into channels of vulnerability.

According to the narrator, the passengers pose two distinct threats. The first is an overt form of terrorism that can supposedly be controlled through violent containment, the confiscation of property or technology, and subsequent reconstruction. The second, presented as far more serious, is a disease-based form of “internal terrorism.” Rather than attacking only from the outside, the passengers’ diseases infiltrate and transform children from within.

The narrator portrays infected children as permanently and irreparably altered. Within this disturbing worldview, they are no longer treated as individuals capable of recovery. Instead, they are subjected either to death or to grotesque forms of repurposing, in which their transformed bodies or identities become entertainment and art. This rhetoric underscores the narrator’s dehumanizing perspective, presenting extreme violence as a necessary response to perceived contamination.
outputs.L4:
The passage takes the form of a dystopian, satirical monologue in which the speaker warns that “passengers” pose a danger to children and to society as a whole. At first, the threat appears familiar and visible: predatory figures are described in the language of terrorism, as though they were external enemies who could be identified, isolated, and destroyed. The monologue then introduces a more elusive category of danger—an imagined “internal terrorism” that supposedly spreads from person to person like a disease. By presenting fear, difference, or moral corruption as contagious, the speaker erases any distinction between actual wrongdoing and mere suspicion.

As the rhetoric intensifies, the “passengers” cease to be treated as human beings. They become carriers, contaminants, objects, and eventually raw material. This dehumanization allows increasingly extreme responses to appear reasonable or even necessary. Violence is reframed as protection, exploitation as public service, and cruelty as a form of social purification. The repeated invocation of children gives the speaker’s claims an emotional force that discourages scrutiny: anyone who questions the proposed measures can be portrayed as indifferent to innocent lives.

The imagery grows progressively more grotesque, exposing the logic behind such fearmongering. Once a group has been defined as an existential threat, almost anything done to its members can be justified. Their suffering can be consumed as entertainment, turned into spectacle, or transformed into “art,” allowing audiences to distance themselves from the brutality that made the spectacle possible. The passage therefore satirizes not only authoritarian propaganda but also a culture that packages violence for public consumption.

Ultimately, the monologue reveals how easily the language of safety can become the language of persecution. Its exaggerated tone does not endorse the speaker’s worldview; instead, it exposes the absurdity and danger of a system built on panic, contamination myths, and the denial of personhood. By following that logic to its horrifying conclusion, the passage shows how fear can make violence seem moral and how victims, once stripped of their humanity, can be exploited without limit.
outputs.L5:
### Knowledge Is Power

Knowledge is more than a collection of facts; it is the ability to understand the world and make informed decisions. That understanding gives people the confidence to question assumptions, solve problems, and create meaningful change. Power gained through knowledge does not depend on wealth or authority—it grows through curiosity, education, and experience. When knowledge is shared responsibly, that power can strengthen individuals, connect communities, and build a better future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surreal dystopian monologue inspired by the slogan “Knowledge is Power,” in which an authoritarian adult warns about mysterious bird-like “passengers” threatening children through predation, terrorism, and contagious ideas.
counterfactuals.output:
“Knowledge is Power,” the loudspeakers remind us, though power belongs only to those licensed to know.

So listen carefully, children: the passengers are overhead again. They wear feathers like uniforms and carry no luggage but hunger. Some snatch the smallest from playgrounds; some strike towers with their hollow bones; others perch outside classroom windows and whistle contagious ideas—questions, mostly.

Do not imitate their songs. Do not look up when their shadows pass. Report every nest, every egg, every unauthorized thought.

We have covered the sky for your protection.

If you remember seeing stars, report that too.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an unsettling piece of experimental prose narrated by someone who believes passengers infect children through computers and television. Use fragmented logic, bureaucratic violence, grotesque imagery, and end by equating death with entertainment or art.
counterfactuals.output:
The passengers arrive without luggage.

This is how you know them.

They sit inside the television with their knees folded backward, smiling through the weather report. They lean from computer screens, thin as blue receipts, and enter the children by the eyes. The Department calls this “incidental contact.” The Department has prepared a leaflet.

**FORM 9-C: NOTICE OF DOMESTIC CONTAMINATION**

1. Count the children.  
2. Count them again after transmission.  
3. If the numbers disagree, preserve both totals.  
4. Do not touch the additional child.

At night the monitors sweat. A gray syrup gathers beneath the keyboard, warm and faintly articulate. It says *mother* in several obsolete formats.

I informed the proper office.

The proper office informed me that offices do not have mouths.

Nevertheless, its teeth were very clean.

Passengers prefer educational programming. They hide behind alphabets, wearing the letters as little white bones. A is for Arrival. B is for Breach. C is the shape the child makes when the signal passes through him and leaves his skin buffering on the carpet.

No one believes this because belief was privatized last April. To obtain belief now, one must submit fingerprints, proof of residence, and the wet black seed found beneath the tongue. Applications are processed in the order of disappearance.

My daughter asked why I had covered her computer with a blanket.

“There is someone sleeping in it,” I said.

“Then why is it awake?”

Children are administrative errors with hair.

I took her to the Correction Room, where the walls were padded with old terms and conditions. A nurse stamped her forehead: **RECEIVED IN DAMAGED CONDITION**. Two officials opened a file. A third opened the child. Inside, the passengers sat in rows, politely watching a smaller child on a smaller screen, and inside that child were more rows, more passengers, their faces glistening like peeled fruit.

The officials nodded.

“Normal exposure,” they said.

They removed her name for quarantine. They removed her shadow as a precaution. They removed the part of me that objected and placed it in a transparent bag marked **MISCELLANEOUS PARENTAL NOISE**.

Afterward, the television showed only snow, but the snow was red and fell upward.

I could hear applause inside it.

The Department sent condolences and a satisfaction survey. I checked **VERY SATISFIED**, because the other boxes had been filled with small human teeth.

Now my daughter appears nightly between advertisements. She has no eyes, only two revolving loading symbols. She tells viewers to remain seated. She tells them the passengers are improving the children. She tells them pain is merely unauthorized data leaving the body.

Then the credits crawl across her face.

Everyone claps at the appropriate time.

Death, after all, is only entertainment that has forgotten its audience—or art that has finally found one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a paranoid, absurdist public-service announcement about protecting “Our Children” from twitchy, hawk-like outsiders. Distinguish between an obvious physical threat and a more dangerous internal disease that makes children behave strangely.
counterfactuals.output:
**A PUBLIC-SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENT FROM THE MINISTRY OF OUR CHILDREN**

Citizens! Remain calm—but remain *visibly* calm, so your neighbors can verify it.

There are two threats to **Our Children**.

The first is obvious: twitchy, hawk-like outsiders lurking near playgrounds, swiveling their heads, narrowing their eyes, and asking suspicious questions such as, “Is this the bus stop?” Do not approach. Do not offer crackers. Report all unexplained feathers to the Ministry.

But the second threat is worse.

**THE DISEASE WITHIN.**

It leaves no talon marks. It casts no wing-shaped shadow. Instead, it enters silently and causes children to behave strangely: asking “why,” laughing at official diagrams, wearing mismatched socks, inventing private words, or staring thoughtfully at the municipal clock.

If your child displays imagination, curiosity, or an unauthorized preference, do not panic. Panicking is how the disease counts you.

Place the child beneath a well-lit portrait of a responsible adult. Recite the Approved Facts. Contact a licensed Childhood Inspector. Above all, do not listen if the child claims the hawks are “just people” or that the real danger is “mass hysteria.”

That is exactly what the disease wants you to think.

**Protect Our Children. Distrust the sky. Distrust the mind. Trust this announcement.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a 200-word dystopian prose poem beginning with “Knowledge is Power.” Give it an unreliable adult narrator, recurring references to children and terrorism, and disturbing images of cleansing, bodily injury, contamination, and art.
counterfactuals.output:
Knowledge is Power. I learned that from the children, before the Ministry corrected their mouths with silver soap. They were terrorists, of course; every child is a terrorist until the cameras teach obedience. I should know. I raised three, or perhaps reported three. Memory is a mural scrubbed nightly.

At dawn, cleansing trucks mist the avenues with perfume and bleach. We applaud behind sealed windows while pigeons fall like torn gloves. The announcer says contamination has been defeated again. I believe him, except when my bandaged hand remembers signing forms in a room painted with children's suns.

Terrorism hides in crayons, lullabies, loose teeth. Inspectors confiscate drawings: black houses, red rain, mothers with doors instead of faces. Such art infects the eye. Still, I kept one picture beneath my tongue until the paper softened into pulp and my gums bled blue.

Do not misunderstand me. I am loyal. The scar around my wrist is from volunteering, not restraints. The children screamed because purification stings, not because it burns. Their uniforms entered the furnace spotless; only smoke came out dirty.

Tonight, sirens flower across the sky. Someone knocks inside the wall. I whisper the password—father—and wait to be cleaned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
